newsitem.title: UK: Conservatives must start again in Scotland, Wales.
newsitem.headline: Conservatives must start again in Scotland, Wales.

text.p: One of the most urgent tasks facing Britain's crushed Conservative party is to restore its credibility in Wales and Scotland, where it lost every single parliamentary seat for the first time in history.

The Conservatives cannot possibly hope to retake power from Labour, which won Thursday's general election by a landslide, without gaining at least a few seats outside England to show they enjoy some support from all parts of the country.

But the scale of the challenge is huge, since all the Conservatives' leading Scots lost their seats, the local hierarchy is in disarray and the party opposes the one policy which could help revive its support - devolved government for Scotland.

Labour was always tipped to do well in the regions given the widespread dislike of the Conservatives but did itself no harm by promising an element of devolution -- giving Wales and Scotland more say over their own affairs.
Activists in Scotland and Wales have long chafed under the Conservatives, accusing the party of treating them as English vassals rather than separate entities.

"The Conservative party is now an English nationalist party, whose electoral support is now almost entirely confined south of the Tweed river (bordering Scotland and England) and Offa's Dyke (on the Welsh-English border)," said the Guardian newspaper.

Labour's proposals, although ground-breaking, are in truth fairly modest -- each region would have its own parliament with limited rights to raise local taxes, but only after the idea was approved by a referendum.
Labour made clear that Britain would stay united but the Conservatives said devolution would split up the "Union" of England, Scotland and Wales and lead to separatism.
Now they may well have to think again.
Arnold Kemp, editor of the Glasgow Herald newspaper from 1981 to 1994, said the party had no choice but to drop its opposition to devolution.
"The Tories lack any moral authority in Scotland. The only route back is to acknowedge the inevitable," he wrote in the Evening Standard newspaper.
David Macletchie, president of the Scottish Conservatives, said opinion polls suggested Scots cared little about devolution but he conceded the party might have to change its stance.
"That's a possibility and the matter has got to be tested in a very full debate which will focus on purely on that particular issue in the referendum," he told BBC radio.
There is little evidence to suggest the Scots or Welsh want full independence, judging by the performance of the parties which officially campaigned to make a clean break with England.

The Scottish National Party gained just six of the 72 Scottish seats while Plaid Cymru ("The Party of Wales") won only four of 40 Welsh seats. Labour took the lion's share with a few going to the minority Liberal Democrats.

The Conservatives will still find it hard to restore their credibility, if only because their new parliamentary spokesmen on Scottish and Welsh affairs will have to be legislators representing seats in England.
To make matters worse, the party in Scotland plunged into scandal just weeks before the election when chairman Sir Michael Hirst resigned after allegations about his private life.
Newspapers strongly hinted that the sources of the story had been Hirst's opponents inside the Scottish Conservative machine, giving the impression of a party at war with itself.

A few days earlier Allan Stewart resigned his position as member of parliament in Scotland's safest Conservative seat after reports linking him to a married woman and an clinic for recovering alcoholics.

But the news for the Conservatives is not all bad. Although the vagaries of Britain's "first-past-the-post" voting system left them without any seats outside England, they got half a million votes in Scotland.

The full title of the party is the Conservative and Unionist party, referring to the 1707 Act of Union which joined Scotland to England to form the United Kingdom. Wales had become part of England in 1536. REUTER
